\section[obtener]{obtener — to obtain, to get}

\label{lesson:ES-C639-obtener}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to control, then the Spanish for except.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: obtener}
\textbf{obtener} — \textquotedblleft{}to obtain, to get\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Obtuvo el mejor resultado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She got the best result.}
\end{quote}

Like \emph{tener}: \emph{obtengo, obtuve}. More formal than \emph{conseguir}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{obtener} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{obtinere} 'to hold, to get', built from \emph{ob} and \emph{tenere} 'to hold', rebuilt on \emph{tener} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{obtener}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{obtener}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{obtener}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to control, then the Spanish for except, then say \emph{obtener} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does obtener mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To obtain, to get\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[abandonar]{abandonar — to abandon, to give up; to leave}

\label{lesson:ES-C639-abandonar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for except, then the Spanish for to obtain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: abandonar}
\textbf{abandonar} — \textquotedblleft{}to abandon, to give up; to leave\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Abandonó los estudios a los dieciocho años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He gave up his studies at eighteen.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Abandonar un proyecto} — to drop a project.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{abandonar} was borrowed from French \emph{abandonner}, from the phrase \emph{à bandon} 'under someone's power', built on a Germanic word for an order, \emph{bannan} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{abandonar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{abandonar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{abandonar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for except, then the Spanish for to obtain, then say \emph{abandonar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does abandonar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To abandon, to give up; to leave\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[rendirse]{rendirse — to give up, to surrender}

\label{lesson:ES-C639-rendirse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to obtain, then the Spanish for to abandon.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rendirse}
\textbf{rendirse} — \textquotedblleft{}to give up, to surrender\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No te rindas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not give up.}
\end{quote}

Like \emph{pedir}: \emph{me rindo, se rindió}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rendirse} is built on \emph{rendir}, inherited from spoken Latin \emph{rendere}, Latin \emph{reddere} 'to give back, to yield' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[asumir]{asumir — to take on; to accept}

\label{lesson:ES-C639-asumir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to abandon, then the Spanish for to give up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: asumir}
\textbf{asumir} — \textquotedblleft{}to take on; to accept\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Asumo la responsabilidad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I take responsibility.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Asumir un riesgo} — to take a risk. It does not usually mean to suppose.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{asumir} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{assumere} 'to take up, to adopt', built from \emph{ad} and \emph{sumere} 'to take' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[exitoso]{exitoso — successful}

\label{lesson:ES-C639-exitoso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to give up, then the Spanish for to take on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: exitoso}
\textbf{exitoso} — \textquotedblleft{}successful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fue un año muy exitoso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It was a very successful year.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{el éxito}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{exitoso} is built on \emph{éxito} with \emph{-oso} (EtymDB); \emph{éxito} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{exitus} 'a going out, an outcome'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[(dialogue)]{Why, and what if — back to the first reasons}

\label{lesson:ES-R639-repaso-por-que-y-si}



\begin{quote}
Two verbs from much earlier in the book: say the Spanish for \textquotedblleft{}to explain\textquotedblright{} and for \textquotedblleft{}must, should\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Te lo explico.} — I'll explain it to you.
  \item a chain of reasons: \emph{Creo que va a llover, así que debo volver a casa.}
  \item the cause, pointed at with \emph{por}: \emph{No salimos por la lluvia.} — We didn't go out because of the rain.
  \item a world that is not real: \emph{Si tuviera tiempo, te lo explicaría.} Then the same with \emph{hiciera}: \emph{Si hiciera buen tiempo, saldríamos.}
  \item an answer that keeps its condition hidden: \emph{¿Vienes mañana? — Depende.} Then name it: \emph{Depende del tiempo.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word points back at a cause, \emph{por} or \emph{para}? (\textbf{Por}.) Which form says \textquotedblleft{}if I had\textquotedblright{}: \emph{tenía} or \emph{tuviera}? (\textbf{Tuviera}.) What does \emph{depende} leave unsaid? (The condition; add \emph{de} to name it.) Say one reason chain of your own with \emph{creo que}, \emph{porque} and \emph{así que}.
\end{tcolorbox}
